newsitem.title: GERMANY: German government postpones decision on petrol tax.
newsitem.headline: German government postpones decision on petrol tax.

text.p: Faced with broad public opposition, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition failed to agree on Thursday on whether to increase the petroleum tax to meet 1997 budget targets and qualify for Europe's single currency.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel warned, however, that there was little room left to cut spending to meet the targets.
"It will be hard to cut the needed five to seven billion marks ($4.5 billion) from the budget," he said outside a parliamentary budget committee meeting.

Government sources said a decision would be reached by Friday on how to plug a public-sector spending gap that could total 10 billion to 11 billion marks when state finances are added in. The shortfall appeared this week due to a rise in child allowance and the elimination of a wealth tax.
The Free Democrats, junior partners in the ruling coalition have voiced opposition to a rise in petroleum tax.

But coalition sources said Waigel had told them they must either accept the idea or the government would have to go back on a decision to lower the "solidarity surcharge" on income tax, levied to help pay for the costs of German unification.
Christian Democrat (CDU) officials said Kohl wanted the issue to be cleared up ahead of his party's congress next week.
Each one-pfennig increase in the petroleum tax could bring federal coffers 700 million marks.
But other officials, including chancellery minister Friedrich Bohl, said the government would rather cut spending than raise taxes.

Earlier this week, Waigel said Germany was still on track to bring its deficit below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 as required by the Maastricht Treaty, in time for the European economic and monetary union in 1999.
Even talking about tax increases hurts the economy, deputy FDP chairman Rainer Bruederle said in a radio interview.

So coalition politicians turned their fire on the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), accusing them of refusing to accept spending cuts proposed by the government or make suitable budget proposals of their own.
The SPD's blockade tactics are "pure show" that hurts the economy and jobs, Waigel said.
The SPD joined the FDP and Greens, business and taxpayer groups, automobile clubs and major newspaper editorialists in rejecting a rise in the petroleum tax.
The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung wrote in an editorial, "Waigel should resist the temptation to fix the 1997 budget with a petroleum tax. The political damage would be enormous."
The tax increase would be blamed on European monetary union and weigh on the future single currency before it even got off the ground, the newspaper said.

Waigel urged the SPD to make its own proposal on the elimination of the capital trading tax, which it has so far opposed. He repeated his offer to raise states' share of value-added taxes as a compensation.
Government parties rejected an SPD motion to advance a planned income tax reform one year to 1998. ($1=1.5390 Mark)
